title: Dynamical structure factor with a pumping approach on a trapped-ion quantum computer
authors: Etienne Granet, Keisuke Murota, Henrik Dreyer, Kentaro Yamamoto, Juan Pedersen, Hidemaro Suwa
abstract: Dynamical structure factors (DSF) measured with neutron-scattering experiments provide key insights into the structure of materials. Their computation requires both the preparation of an equilibrium state and the implementation of Hamiltonian dynamics. We demonstrate the feasibility of computing DSF on the Quantinuum Reimei trapped-ion quantum computer, comparing the DSF of 1D Heisenberg model on $20$ sites, and that of the copper sulfate crystal. To that end, we introduce a pumping approach for computing the DSF $S(q,ω)$ on quantum computers that enables targeting specific arbitrary values of frequencies $ω$. This method time-evolves the initial state using a time-dependent Hamiltonian perturbed by a source term oscillating at the target frequency $ω$. When targeting only a few frequency values, this approach provides a significant reduction in shot overhead compared to previous methods.
summary: This paper presents a novel 'pumping approach' to calculate the Dynamical Structure Factor, $S(q, \omega)$, which is vital for understanding material structure from neutron scattering. The technique is demonstrated using a trapped-ion quantum computer platform to simulate models like the 1D Heisenberg chain. It shows that this method efficiently targets specific frequencies and yields results matching both simulations and experimental expectations.
main_problem: The primary goal is computing Dynamical Structure Factors (DSF), $S(q, \omega)$, which are crucial for interpreting neutron-scattering experiments on materials.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated the feasibility of calculating DSF using a novel 'pumping approach' directly on a trapped-ion quantum computer platform.
method: They introduce a pumping technique that uses time evolution with a source term oscillating at the target frequency $\omega$ to measure $S(q, \omega)$, significantly reducing overhead compared to older methods.
model_or_system: The study applies this method to model systems like the 1D Heisenberg chain (relevant to copper sulfate) and tests it on the Quantinuum Reimei trapped-ion quantum computer.
key_observables: Dynamical Structure Factor, $S(q, \omega)$; relative energy difference between ansatz and ground state; error metrics related to $\epsilon$ and time truncation $T$.
important_parameters: System size ($L=20$), Trotter step ($dt=0.24$), total evolution time ($T=2.4$), and the coupling parameter ($\epsilon$).
main_assumptions: The method relies on approximating the infinite-time limit via finite truncation (introducing sinc function artifacts) and uses an adiabatic-inspired ansatz for state preparation.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the influence of time evolution approximations on excitation energies, track the convergence of the optimized ansatz energy to the ground state energy, and compare measured DSF results against noiseless simulations and experimental data.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the physical problem (DSF), details the novel pumping methodology for quantum computation, describes the implementation using trapped-ion hardware, presents comparisons with theoretical benchmarks, and concludes with validation of the approach.
why_interesting: This work directly bridges fundamental condensed matter physics observables (like DSF) with cutting-edge quantum hardware capabilities (trapped ions), offering a concrete roadmap for simulating complex many-body dynamics on NISQ devices.
